reviews.review:
SoulHunt is an asymmetric multiplayer game built around the simple pleasure of hiding, hunting, and trying to outsmart other players. Developed and published by WinterCell Studios, it takes inspiration from prop-hunting games but attempts to give the formula more personality through character abilities and different match types. One team hides by blending into the environment, while the opposing seekers search for anything that looks suspicious. The premise is easy to understand, making it the sort of multiplayer game that can produce entertaining moments without requiring players to spend hours learning complicated systems.

The hiding side provides much of the game's tension and humor. Becoming part of the scenery sounds straightforward, but surviving requires choosing believable positions and anticipating how experienced seekers inspect a room. A hiding place that initially seems perfect can quickly become dangerous when an opponent begins checking objects nearby. This creates an enjoyable psychological element where patience is just as useful as movement. Sometimes remaining completely still is the safest strategy, while other situations encourage a risky escape or repositioning attempt.

Playing as a seeker offers a noticeably different experience. Instead of simply wandering around and attacking random objects, players have access to abilities intended to help locate their targets. Different seeker characters bring their own skills, adding some variety to how the hunting side approaches each round. Observation remains important because understanding the natural arrangement of objects can expose a poorly disguised opponent. This makes map knowledge increasingly valuable as players become familiar with each environment.

SoulHunt includes three maps and three game modes, giving the basic concept several ways to play. The amount of content is relatively modest, however, especially for a game centered on repeated multiplayer matches. Maps in a prop-hunting game are particularly important because their effectiveness gradually changes as players memorize object placement and discover popular hiding locations. Greater environmental variety would have helped preserve the sense of uncertainty that makes the opening hours entertaining.

The game originally entered Early Access with considerably larger ambitions. Plans included additional seekers, more types of hiders, new abilities, further game modes, and a level editor that could have allowed the community to build and share its own maps. Such features would have been particularly valuable for a game dependent on replayability. Unfortunately, development did not progress as originally expected, and the project has remained in Early Access for years without receiving the continued support necessary to fully realize those ideas. As a result, it is better evaluated according to the content already present rather than the features once envisioned for its future.

Presentation is functional rather than spectacular. The environments mainly exist to support hiding and searching, and the visuals reflect the modest scope of the project. The darker atmosphere gives the game a slight horror flavor, but SoulHunt is not primarily about delivering frightening encounters. Its entertainment comes from the unpredictable behavior of other players. Watching a seeker walk past your hiding place or suddenly realizing that an ordinary object is actually another player creates the kind of spontaneous situations that scripted content would struggle to reproduce.

Hardware requirements are very modest, which makes SoulHunt accessible to older PCs. It was designed around relatively lightweight specifications and does not demand a modern gaming system. The game also supports online PvP and cross-platform multiplayer and includes Steam achievements, statistics, trading cards, and in-game chat. These additions complement the multiplayer focus, although their value naturally depends on being able to find other people to play with.

Steam Deck compatibility is currently not officially rated by Valve, meaning SoulHunt should be regarded as Steam Deck Unknown rather than Verified or Playable. Its relatively modest system requirements may suggest that the hardware itself is capable enough, but that does not guarantee trouble-free operation through SteamOS. Controller behavior, interface readability, multiplayer functionality, and compatibility can all affect the handheld experience. Players specifically purchasing it for Steam Deck should therefore expect that additional configuration or experimentation may be necessary.

SoulHunt ultimately feels like a promising multiplayer concept that never received enough development to reach its full potential. The mixture of prop hiding, specialized abilities, observation, and player-driven deception can still create amusing and tense matches. The problem is that limited content and prolonged inactivity make the experience considerably less compelling than the original concept suggests. Since it is free to play, curious players can experiment with it without a financial commitment, particularly if they already have friends willing to join them. As a snapshot of an ambitious indie multiplayer project, there is still some enjoyment here, but its unfinished state remains impossible to overlook.

Rating: 6/10
